label: Stage 0
name: Math foundations
why: Every later derivation, from attention to scaling-law fits to DPO’s loss, is built from these pieces.
tst: Check every hand-derived gradient against finite differences in a test that runs automatically.
holds: Most of ML is a few pieces of math used over and over: vectors and matrix multiplies, probability, derivatives, and lowering a loss by stepping downhill.
breaks: Nothing breaks yet. Skipping this is what makes the attention and scaling-law derivations feel like magic later.

project.title: Regression from scratch
project.brief: Using only NumPy, fit linear regression three ways, then logistic regression with gradients you derived on paper. Finish with PCA from the eigenvectors of a covariance matrix.
ms: Derive the gradient of mean squared error by hand and check it with finite differences
Fit linear regression with the normal equations and with gradient descent; confirm they agree
Logistic regression on a 2-class dataset using your hand-derived cross-entropy gradient
Sweep 5 learning rates and plot the loss curves; find where training diverges
PCA on a small dataset from the covariance matrix’s eigenvectors; plot the first two components

predict: Before the sweep, guess the largest learning rate that won’t diverge.
explain: Explain why cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the data, using a coin-flip example.
revisit: Nothing to revisit yet. Start the error log here.

work: Tracing why a recommendation model’s gradients explode after a new feature ships, and fixing the math
Compressing millions of product embeddings with PCA before indexing them for search
Explaining to leadership why a demand forecast’s uncertainty widened this quarter

readings.title: Essence of Linear Algebra
readings.note: Visual intuition for vectors, matrices, determinants and eigenvectors. Watch before the textbook.

readings.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
readings.note: Free textbook. Read chapters 2 to 7: linear algebra, matrix decompositions, vector calculus, probability and optimization.

readings.title: The Matrix Calculus You Need for Deep Learning
readings.note: Gradients of vector and matrix expressions, written for people who build networks.

readings.title: Seeing Theory
readings.note: Interactive visual introduction to probability and statistics. The site is archived but still available.

readings.title: CS229 lecture notes
readings.note: Linear and logistic regression, maximum likelihood and generalized linear models, derived step by step.

label: Stage 1
name: Neural nets & autograd
why: Autograd is the chain rule from Stage 0 turned into code, and every project after this trains something.
sec: Saved PyTorch .pt files are pickles that can run code when loaded. Load downloaded weights with weights_only=True, or use safetensors.
tst: Test shapes, gradients and a one-batch overfit. These three checks catch most model bugs.
holds: A neural network is a differentiable program. Stack simple functions, measure the loss, and autograd gives you the gradient of everything.
breaks: Autograd gives you gradients, not good training. Whether a model learns anything useful is a data and training-dynamics question, covered in Stages 2 and 4.

project.title: Micrograd replay
project.brief: Rebuild a scalar autograd engine from memory, then use it to train a small MLP. Check every gradient against PyTorch.
ms: Value class with +, *, tanh and a backward() that walks a topological sort
Gradient check: match PyTorch to 1e-6 on a random expression
Train a 2-layer MLP on a toy 2D dataset to >95% accuracy
Rewrite the training loop in PyTorch and confirm identical loss curves

predict: Before running backward(), compute one weight’s gradient by hand and write it down.
explain: Explain why gradients are summed when a value feeds two operations.
revisit: Redo your Stage 0 logistic regression as a one-neuron network in your engine. Do the gradients match your hand derivation?

work: Writing a custom layer and its gradient for a ranking model, then proving it matches a reference implementation
Porting a production model between frameworks and showing outputs match to 1e-6
Building shared training pipelines that dozens of internal teams reuse

readings.title: Intro to backprop (micrograd)
readings.note: Builds autograd from scratch in about two hours. The template for this whole syllabus: build first, then explain.

readings.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
readings.note: The video series that leads into the GPT build in Stage 3.

readings.title: Adam
readings.note: The optimizer behind nearly every model on this map. Skim the update rule and bias correction.

readings.title: Deep Learning (book)
readings.note: Free reference text. Chapter 6 (feedforward networks) and chapter 8 (optimization) pair with this stage.

label: Stage 2
name: Data & evaluation
why: Comes before any big model, so every number you report from here on has an honest split, a baseline and an error bar.
sec: Data leakage has a privacy twin: keep real people’s data out of public repos, and treat test sets that contain it as sensitive.
tst: Write tests that fail if any example appears in two splits, if the schema changes, or if label balance shifts sharply.
holds: A model is only as good as its data and the test that measures it. A clean held-out split, a strong baseline and an honest metric catch most bad conclusions.
breaks: Benchmarks leak into training data, test sets get reused until they are overfit, and small score differences are often noise. A number without an error bar and a contamination check is a rumor.

project.title: Leak hunt
project.brief: Train a simple classifier on a real dataset, then deliberately add four kinds of leakage and measure how much each one inflates the score. Finish by comparing two models with bootstrap confidence intervals and checking a benchmark for contamination.
ms: Make train, validation and test splits; write down what the test set is for and lock it away
Train baselines (majority class, then logistic regression) and record their scores
Add leakage four ways: duplicates across splits, a target-derived feature, preprocessing fit on all data, and a time-order violation; measure each inflation
Compute bootstrap 95% intervals for two models and decide whether the gap is real
Check a small public benchmark against a text corpus for 13-gram overlap and report the contamination rate
Write pytest tests for your data pipeline (no example in two splits, schema and label checks) and have them run automatically on every push

predict: Guess which leak inflates accuracy the most before running any of them.
explain: Explain to a non-engineer why a 0.5-point leaderboard gain may mean nothing.
revisit: Re-run your Stage 1 MLP with a proper validation split. Was it overfitting?

work: Owning the eval suite that must pass before any model release ships at an AI lab
Auditing a fraud model that looked 99% accurate and finding target leakage
Running contamination checks before a company publishes benchmark results
Writing the launch criteria (metrics, error bars, regressions) a program review signs off on

readings.title: Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science
readings.note: A taxonomy of eight leakage types found across hundreds of published papers. Use it as your project checklist.

readings.title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
readings.note: Rebuilt the ImageNet test set and found every model scored lower. A lesson in test-set reuse and subtle shift.

readings.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals
readings.note: How to report language-model eval results with standard errors, clustered questions and paired comparisons.

readings.title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList
readings.note: Invariance, directional and minimum-functionality tests for models, borrowed from software testing.

readings.title: Datasheets for Datasets
readings.note: Questions every dataset should answer: who made it, what is in it, and what it should not be used for.

readings.title: HELM
readings.note: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models. Many scenarios and many metrics instead of one leaderboard number.

readings.title: MMLU
readings.note: A widely used multiple-choice knowledge benchmark. Good for practicing contamination checks.

readings.title: Time Travel in LLMs: Tracing Data Contamination
readings.note: Methods for detecting whether a model has seen a benchmark during training.

readings.title: The ML Test Score
readings.note: A 28-item rubric for testing data, models, infrastructure and monitoring in production ML.

readings.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
readings.note: Why the model is the small part of a production ML system, and where the hidden maintenance costs come from.

label: Track D
name: Ads & growth ML
why: Needs only math and evaluation, so it starts right after Stage 2. It runs on tabular data, so your Mac is enough, and it gives the agency CRM a working lead-scoring model early.
serves: the ad marketplace, the agency CRM
sec: Housing, job and credit ads have legal limits on targeting by protected traits and close stand-ins such as zip code. Check lookalike features for proxies.
tst: Test feature code for leakage: assert that no feature uses information from after the moment of prediction.
holds: Most business ML runs on tables, not text. Gradient-boosted trees on well-built features beat deep models on most tabular problems, and calibrated probabilities turn predictions into budget decisions.
breaks: Prediction isn’t causation. A model that predicts who converts doesn’t tell you which ad caused the sale, and optimizing on observed clicks bakes in the platform’s own targeting. Proving that spend worked takes experiments or careful causal methods.

project.title: Ad marketplace campaign brain
project.brief: Using a public ad dataset plus your agency’s own records, predict conversion, allocate a simulated budget across channels with a bandit, and estimate the true lift of one campaign. The lead-scoring model feeds the agency CRM.
ms: Train logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees on a public click-through dataset; compare log loss and AUC with bootstrap intervals
Calibrate the better model and plot a reliability diagram; write down why calibration matters for bidding
Score your own past leads for likelihood to book, then check feature importances for leakage
Simulate 5 channels with hidden conversion rates; compare a fixed split, epsilon-greedy and Thompson sampling on total conversions
Design an A/B test for one real campaign: power analysis, sample size, and the analysis plan written before you see results
Estimate lift on a public uplift dataset with a two-model approach, and compare it with the naive difference

predict: Predict how many simulated days Thompson sampling needs to find the best channel.
explain: Explain to a client why “people who saw the ad bought more” doesn’t prove the ad worked.
revisit: Run your Stage 2 leakage checklist on the lead-scoring features. Which one would give away the outcome?

work: Click-through-rate models that score billions of ad auctions a day at an ad platform
Geo-lift and holdout studies that prove a campaign’s return to a large advertiser
Marketing mix models that set a retailer’s quarterly budget across channels
Lead-scoring models inside enterprise CRMs that route sales teams to the best accounts

readings.title: XGBoost
readings.note: The scalable gradient-boosting system. Skim the method; use the library.

readings.title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?
readings.note: The evidence for starting with trees.

readings.title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments
readings.note: The standard book on A/B testing in practice.

readings.title: A Tutorial on Thompson Sampling
readings.note: Bandits explained with worked examples.

readings.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
readings.note: Why modern models are overconfident, and temperature scaling as a fix.

readings.title: DLRM
readings.note: Deep Learning Recommendation Model. How large ad and recommendation models are built.

readings.title: Causal Inference: The Mixtape (online edition, now The Remix)
readings.note: Free, readable book on causal methods for observational data.

readings.title: Causal Inference and Uplift Modeling: A Review
readings.note: Short survey of uplift methods, including the two-model approach in the project.

label: Stage 3
name: Transformers & scaling laws
why: You now have the math to derive attention and the evaluation habits to trust your own scaling fit.
sec: Language models memorize rare training text, so anything private in your training data can come back out.
tst: Test the causal mask (no token can see the future) and that loss on one tiny batch drops near zero.
holds: Attention plus scale explains most recent language-model progress. Loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute.
breaks: Kaplan’s compute allocation was revised by Chinchilla, which found tokens matter about as much as parameters. Scaling laws count FLOPs and say nothing about how long a FLOP takes on real hardware.

project.title: Tiny GPT and a scaling sweep
project.brief: Write a decoder-only transformer without nn.Transformer, train it on a small text corpus, then train five sizes and fit a power law to final loss.
ms: Single-head causal self-attention with a visible mask test
Multi-head attention, MLP, residuals and LayerNorm assembled into blocks
Train to a validation loss that beats a bigram baseline by a wide margin
Train 5 model sizes on the same token budget and log FLOPs with 6·N·D
Fit loss vs parameters on a log-log plot and report the exponent

predict: Guess the fitted exponent and the size where your curve flattens before you fit anything.
explain: Explain scaled dot-product attention, including the √dₖ, to someone who knows matrix multiplication.
revisit: Report your validation loss across three seeds with a bootstrap interval. Is the gap over the bigram baseline real?

work: Running small scaling-law sweeps that decide how big the next flagship model should be
Forecasting how many GPUs and weeks a training run needs, months in advance
Pretraining a domain model on a bank’s or hospital’s own text

readings.title: Attention Is All You Need
readings.note: The transformer paper. Read section 3 three times and re-derive the attention equation from a blank page.

readings.title: Let’s build GPT
readings.note: Watch once, then rebuild without the video. The rebuild is the Stage 3 project.

readings.title: Scaling Laws for Neural LMs
readings.note: The original power-law fits. Focus on the figures and the compute-allocation argument.

readings.title: Chinchilla
readings.note: Training Compute-Optimal LLMs. Revises Kaplan: about 20 tokens per parameter.

readings.title: nanochat (successor to nanoGPT)
readings.note: Karpathy’s current compact reference for training a small chat model end to end. Diff your GPT against it. His older nanoGPT repo is now marked deprecated.

readings.title: GPT-3
readings.note: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners. What scale bought in practice.

readings.title: RoFormer (RoPE)
readings.note: Rotary position embeddings, the default in most current open models.

readings.title: Neural MT of Rare Words with Subword Units (BPE)
readings.note: Introduced byte-pair encoding for neural models. Short and readable.

readings.title: Stanford CS336 (Spring 2026)
readings.note: Language Modeling from Scratch, with recorded lectures. Its five assignments make good deep-path versions of Stages 3, 5, 8 and 10.

label: Stage 4
name: Training dynamics
why: Follows the transformer because you now have a real model whose training you can break and fix.
sec: A few bad training examples can plant a hidden trigger. Know where every training file came from.
tst: Run the same short training twice with the same seed and assert the losses match. Unrepeatable runs hide real bugs.
holds: Most training failures are recipe problems, not architecture problems. Learning rate, warmup, initialization, batch size and numeric precision decide whether a good model trains at all.
breaks: Rules of thumb don’t transfer across scale. The best learning rate shifts as models grow, loss spikes show up mostly in big runs, and a run that looks fine on training loss can be quietly overfitting.

project.title: Break it, then fix it
project.brief: Take your Stage 3 GPT and break training five ways. Diagnose each failure from the loss curve and gradient statistics alone, then fix it. End with a learning-rate sweep at two model widths.
ms: Log loss, gradient norm, learning rate and weight norms every step to a dashboard such as TensorBoard
Break it five ways: learning rate 10× too high, no warmup, bad initialization, no gradient clipping, fp16 without loss scaling; screenshot each failure
Fix each one and write a one-line diagnosis rule per failure
Overfit one tiny batch to prove the model can learn, then add weight decay or dropout and show the train–validation gap shrink
Sweep the learning rate at two model widths and plot how the best value moves

predict: Predict whether the best learning rate goes up or down when you double model width.
explain: Explain warmup to someone who has never trained a model.
revisit: Do your Stage 3 scaling fits change when each size gets its own tuned learning rate?

work: Monitoring a multi-week run on thousands of GPUs and rewinding to a checkpoint after a loss spike
Tuning hyperparameters on small proxy models so settings transfer to the full-size run
Building the dashboards and alerts that catch divergence before it wastes a week of compute

readings.title: A Recipe for Training Neural Networks
readings.note: A practical debugging process: inspect data, overfit one batch, then add complexity one step at a time.

readings.title: Deep Learning Tuning Playbook
readings.note: How to tune learning rate, batch size and schedules systematically instead of by luck.

readings.title: Mixed Precision Training
readings.note: fp16 training with fp32 master weights and loss scaling. Read why gradients underflow.

readings.title: Decoupled Weight Decay (AdamW)
readings.note: Why weight decay should be separate from Adam’s gradient scaling.

readings.title: Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD
readings.note: Linear learning-rate scaling with batch size, plus gradual warmup.

readings.title: Delving Deep into Rectifiers
readings.note: The initialization scheme that keeps ReLU networks trainable.

readings.title: Tensor Programs V (μP)
readings.note: Tuning large networks by tuning small ones. Skim the figures showing the best LR staying put across widths.

readings.title: Dropout
readings.note: Randomly dropping units during training to reduce overfitting.

label: Stage 5
name: Post-training
why: Needs a pretrained model, training-dynamics instincts and evaluation discipline, which Stages 2 to 4 just gave you.
hwt: Mac with MLX for LoRA; a rented GPU makes DPO much faster
sec: Preference tuning shapes safety behavior. Measure refusals and harmful outputs before and after tuning, not just helpfulness.
tst: Keep a fixed set of prompts and check every new checkpoint against it before you keep it.
holds: A pretrained model knows a lot but doesn’t follow instructions. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the format, and preference tuning (RLHF or DPO) pushes it toward answers people prefer, using a small fraction of pretraining compute.
breaks: Preference tuning optimizes a stand-in for what people want. Push too hard and the model learns to please the reward model (reward hacking), drifts from its base knowledge, or gets wordier without getting better. Catching that takes Stage 2 discipline.

project.title: Instruct-tune a small model
project.brief: Fine-tune a small open model (about 0.5 to 1B parameters) with LoRA on an instruction dataset, then run DPO on a preference dataset. Evaluate each step against the base model on held-out prompts.
ms: Run the base model on 50 held-out prompts and save the outputs as your baseline
Supervised fine-tune with LoRA on an instruction dataset; plot training and validation loss
Run DPO on a preference dataset, starting from your fine-tuned checkpoint
Compare base, SFT and DPO by win rate (LLM-as-a-judge with answer order swapped) and one exact-match task, with bootstrap intervals
Find a reward-hacking or length-bias symptom in your DPO outputs and document it
Deep path: write a verifiable RL environment (for example, a checker that scores storyboard shot lists against a script) and run a small GRPO loop with TRL on a rented GPU

predict: Predict the DPO-vs-SFT win rate and how much average answer length will change.
explain: Explain the difference between RLHF and DPO in three sentences, without equations.
revisit: Put your Stage 4 dashboard on the fine-tuning run. Which training failure is most likely at this scale?

work: Running preference-data programs with thousands of annotators and quality checks
Fine-tuning a customer-support model to follow one company’s policies and tone
Training reasoning models with verifiable rewards on code and math

readings.title: InstructGPT
readings.note: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. The SFT → reward model → PPO pipeline.

readings.title: Direct Preference Optimization
readings.note: Shows the RLHF objective can be optimized with a simple classification-style loss on preference pairs.

readings.title: LoRA
readings.note: Low-rank adaptation. Read the parameter-count comparison and the rank ablation.

readings.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
readings.note: The RL algorithm used in classic RLHF. Skim the clipped objective.

readings.title: Constitutional AI
readings.note: Replacing much human preference labeling with AI feedback guided by written principles.

readings.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench)
readings.note: Measures how well model judges agree with people, and documents their biases.

readings.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
readings.note: How true quality first rises and then falls as you optimize harder against a reward model.

readings.title: Tülu 3
readings.note: A fully open post-training recipe: SFT, DPO and RL with verifiable rewards, with data and code.

readings.title: DeepSeek-R1
readings.note: Reasoning ability from large-scale RL with verifiable rewards.

readings.title: TRL library docs
readings.note: The library you’ll likely use for SFT and DPO in the project.

readings.title: DeepSeekMath (introduces GRPO)
readings.note: The paper behind GRPO, the critic-free RL method most reasoning models now use. Read the GRPO section.

readings.title: Toy Models of Superposition
readings.note: Why single neurons rarely mean one thing. The foundation for sparse autoencoders.

readings.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
readings.note: Attribution graphs that trace how a production model reaches specific answers.

readings.title: circuit-tracer
readings.note: Open library for building attribution graphs on open-weight models. Optional hands-on follow-up.

label: Track C
name: LLM applications
why: Follows Stage 5 because you now know what fine-tuning and judges can and can’t do, so you can choose between prompting, retrieval and tuning.
serves: the agency CRM, the storyboard app, the video editor
hwt: Mac plus API credits; a small cloud server to deploy
sec: Agents that read the web can be hijacked by hidden instructions. Give tools the least access they need and require approval for anything irreversible. Track S goes deeper.
tst: Every prompt or model change reruns the eval set. Block the change if scores drop beyond the error bars.
holds: Most of an LLM product’s value comes from the system around the model: structured outputs your code can trust, retrieval that grounds answers in your own data, tools the model can call, and evals that catch regressions.
breaks: LLM apps fail quietly. Retrieval misses the right document, agents loop or take the wrong action, and outputs shift when the model changes. Without an eval set and logged traces, you can’t tell whether a prompt change helped. In production, an agent that can act also needs limits on what it may do and spend.

project.title: Agency CRM proposal agent
project.brief: Build an agent that reads a lead’s website, extracts structured facts, retrieves your most relevant past projects, and drafts a proposal and landing-page copy. An eval set scores every version, and the finished agent is deployed with limits, approvals and monitoring.
ms: Extract company name, industry, size signals and contact page into a validated JSON schema from 50 real websites; measure field accuracy
Index your past proposals and project notes; build retrieval with embeddings plus keyword search; measure recall@5 on 30 queries you write
Draft proposals grounded in the retrieved projects, citing which past project each claim came from
Add tools (a pricing calculator, calendar availability) and log a full trace of every run
Build a 40-case eval set with rubric-based LLM judging, spot-check it against your own grades, and compare two prompt versions with bootstrap intervals
Add guardrails against inventing clients or prices, and test them with adversarial inputs, including instructions hidden in a lead’s website
Package your tools as an MCP server and connect the agent to it, so the storyboard app and the video editor can reuse them
Deploy the agent behind an API with per-run cost and time limits, retries, human approval before anything is sent to a lead, and a dashboard of traces and eval scores

Decision-layer bake-off: qualify 300 leads three ways (a small fine-tuned classifier, a frontier LLM with structured output, and a System One decision model, either TypeSafe’s hosted Jev or an open-weight one such as Amazon’s Strands Decider 2B running on your Mac); compare accuracy with bootstrap intervals, calibration (Brier score and a reliability diagram), p95 latency and cost per 1,000 decisions

predict: Predict your retrieval recall@5 before you measure it.
explain: Explain when to fine-tune, when to retrieve and when to just rewrite the prompt.
revisit: Apply Stage 5’s judge-bias fixes to your eval. Does swapping answer order change the result?

roles: Customer program manager for AI deployments
work: Deploying an internal knowledge assistant over company documents, with access controls per team
Building agents that triage support tickets and draft replies, with a human approving each send
Running evals and red-teaming before an enterprise customer goes live
Leading a customer’s rollout program: success metrics, pilot groups, risk reviews and adoption reporting

label: Track S
name: Security, privacy & safety
why: Comes right after Track C, the first time you ship something that reads untrusted input and takes actions, and before the tracks that handle client footage, faces and voices.
serves: the ad marketplace, the storyboard app, the video editor, the agency CRM
tst: Keep your 30 attacks as an automated test suite and rerun it on every change to the agent.
holds: Most ML security failures are ordinary security failures in a new place: untrusted input, permissions that are too broad, leaked secrets and unvetted dependencies. Threat modeling, least privilege and red-teaming your own system catch most of them.
breaks: ML adds attacks ordinary security tools don’t see: instructions hidden in data, poisoned training sets, model files that run code when loaded, and models that leak what they were trained on. Safety failures, such as discriminatory ad targeting or deceptive generated media, cause harm even when nothing is breached.

project.title: Red-team your own agent
project.brief: Threat-model the proposal agent from Track C, attack it the way an adversary would, fix what you find, and write the one-page security and privacy review an enterprise customer’s security team would ask for.
ms: Threat-model the agent against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2026): list its assets, entry points, tools and exactly what each tool may do
Red-team it with 30 attacks, including instructions hidden in a lead’s website, data exfiltration through tool calls, and attempts to make it quote unapproved prices; record the success rate
Fix the top three problems (least-privilege tools, approval gates, output checks) and re-run the same 30 attacks to measure the improvement
Secure the supply chain: load models only as safetensors, pin dependency versions, scan for secrets, and show with a harmless demo why loading an untrusted pickle file runs code
Run a membership-inference test on a small model fine-tuned on private text, then retrain with deduplication or differential privacy and compare
Write a one-page security, privacy and responsible-use review: data handled, retention, consent for faces and voices, ad-targeting rules, and how generated media is labeled

predict: Predict what share of your 30 attacks will succeed before you run them.
explain: Explain indirect prompt injection to a non-technical client, and why a better prompt can’t fully fix it.
revisit: Go back to your Stage 2 leakage checklist. Which of those leaks would also be a privacy breach if the data were about real people?

work: Red-teaming a new model or agent before launch and tracking every finding to a fix
Running the AI risk review that every customer-facing AI feature must pass, mapped to NIST AI RMF
Answering enterprise customers’ security questionnaires about how their data is used in AI features
Detecting and removing deepfake and scam ads on an ad platform

label: Stage 6
name: Convolution & inductive bias
why: Placed here so the CNN-vs-ViT comparison uses proper evaluation, and because the CNN and ViT backbones are what Tracks B and A build on. It also sets up a question the systems stages answer: why is convolution so cheap?
sec: Vision models can be fooled by tiny, invisible pixel changes, so never use one alone for a security decision.
tst: Add behavioral tests: a flipped or slightly cropped image should get the same label.
holds: Convolution builds in locality and weight sharing, so it needs less data, and each weight is reused at every position, which keeps arithmetic intensity high.
breaks: ViT showed that weak priors win once data is large enough, and ConvNeXt showed much of the remaining gap was training recipe. Inductive bias is a trade against data, not a law.

label: Track B
name: Video & audio understanding
why: Follows Stage 6 because these models are built on CNN and ViT backbones, and it comes before Track A because masks, depth and pose are what you use to control generation.
serves: the video editor, the storyboard app
hwt: Mac; a cloud GPU speeds up long clips
sec: Face and voice data counts as biometric data in many places, with consent and retention rules. Get written consent and keep it in your private repo.
tst: Keep hand-labeled clips from your own footage as a fixed test set, and never tune on them.
holds: Pretrained models now handle most perception tasks out of the box: segment and track an object, estimate depth and motion, embed frames for search, and transcribe speech with word timings.
breaks: Real footage breaks them at the edges: motion blur, low light, fast cuts, overlapping speakers, music under dialogue. Errors also build up over time, so a mask that drifts two pixels a frame is useless after ten seconds.

label: Track A
name: Generative vision
why: Comes after Track B, so you already have the masks, depth maps and poses that control generation, and after Stage 5, so LoRA and preference tuning carry over.
serves: the storyboard app, the video editor
hwt: Cloud NVIDIA GPU for video models; Mac for image work
sec: Generated media can deceive. Label it, keep provenance metadata (C2PA), and never generate real people without permission.
tst: Generate with fixed seeds and reference images so you can see when a change alters identity or style.
holds: Diffusion and flow-matching models make images by learning to undo noise step by step. Working in a compressed latent space makes this affordable, and conditioning signals such as text, pose, depth and reference images give you control.
breaks: Control is the hard part. Text prompts don’t pin down identity, camera or layout; characters drift between shots; video models flicker; and every denoising step is a full model pass, so speed and consistency trade against each other.

label: Stage 7
name: GPU execution & profiling
why: Moved ahead of IO-aware kernels. You need to read a trace and understand async launches before a roofline means anything.
hwt: Mac (Instruments) plus a few hours on a rented NVIDIA GPU for Nsight
sec: Rented GPU machines are on the internet. Never expose Jupyter without a password, and keep API keys out of notebooks.
tst: Add a benchmark test that fails if a training step gets more than 10% slower.
holds: CUDA launches are asynchronous. When kernels are large, Python races ahead and its cost is hidden.
breaks: When kernels are tiny, as in small-batch decode, or when code hits a sync point like .item(), the GPU sits idle waiting for Python. The gaps are visible in an Nsight trace.

label: Stage 8
name: IO-aware kernels
why: The FlashAttention beat lands better now: you can already see memory traffic in a trace, and here you write the fused kernel that removes it.
hwt: Mac for the Metal path, or a rented NVIDIA GPU for the Triton path
tst: Test every kernel against the PyTorch version for correctness before you time it.
holds: Softmax, LayerNorm, elementwise ops and long-sequence attention are memory-bound. FlashAttention wins by cutting reads and writes to HBM, while doing slightly more FLOPs.
breaks: Large training matmuls are compute-bound. “FLOPs don’t matter” is only true to the left of the roofline’s ridge point, and the roofline tells you which side you are on.

project.title: Roofline your GPU, then write the kernel

Then write one fused kernel: Triton on a rented NVIDIA GPU, or Metal through MLX on your Mac. A fused color-grade kernel is the Metal option, and it is directly useful for the video editor. Runs at measure-and-reason depth: two weeks, one kernel.

label: Stage 9
name: Mixture of experts
why: Needs your GPT, your roofline and your evaluation habits. MoE claims are about loss per FLOP and bytes moved, and both need honest measurement.
tst: Test that the router sends each token to exactly k experts and that the balancing loss stays finite.
holds: MoE separates total parameters from FLOPs per token. DeepSeek-V3 reported a competitive model at a training compute budget far below comparable dense models.
breaks: Every expert still has to be stored and moved. MoE adds memory cost, all-to-all communication and load-balancing problems, and at large decode batches nearly every expert gets touched.

label: Stage 10
name: Inference at scale
why: The capstone pulls everything together: bandwidth floors (Stage 8), launch overhead (7), active parameters (9) and quality checks (2). The same latency model prices serving for the video editor and the storyboard app.
hwt: Rented NVIDIA GPUs for serving tests; Mac for your own GPT
sec: Serving endpoints need authentication, rate limits and spending caps, or a leaked key becomes a large bill.
tst: Load-test the endpoint at rising request rates and alert on latency, errors and output drift.
holds: CUDA graphs record a sequence of kernel launches and replay it as one, removing per-launch CPU overhead. At batch 1 with thousands of small kernels, that overhead is real.
breaks: CUDA graphs remove overhead above a floor. The floor is bytes moved per token divided by memory bandwidth, set by size, precision, sharding, batch and whether the model is MoE. At bf16, 400B parameters is 800 GB of weights, more than eight 80 GB H100s hold.
